courseInfo.description: You can already build a single agent that calls tools in a loop. But some problems are too big for one agent: a customer-support request that needs billing, technical, and returns expertise; a report that must be researched, drafted, then edited. This course is the entry point to multi-agent systems. You will learn to reason about when to split work across specialized agents versus keeping one well-equipped agent, name the flow patterns that structure multi-agent workflows, and take the concrete first implementation step: replacing hand-written tool-dispatch loops with a ToolNode, and letting tools read from and write to shared graph state. All code targets LangGraph 1.2.8 using the exact pinned imports.

Course description
You can already build a single agent that calls tools in a loop. But some problems are too big for one agent: a
customer-support request that needs billing, technical, and returns expertise; a report that must be
researched, drafted, then edited. This course is the entry point to multi-agent systems — you'll learn to reason
about when to split work across specialized agents versus keeping one well-equipped agent, name the flow
patterns that structure multi-agent workflows, and take the concrete first implementation step: replacing
hand-written tool-dispatch loops with a ToolNode , and letting tools read from and write to shared graph
state.
Course philosophy
One purpose per agent beats one agent that does everything — structure is what keeps complexity
from breaking a system
Agents coordinate through a shared, typed state (a blackboard) and structured handoffs, never
through free-form guesswork
Start from the smallest concrete step ( ToolNode , scoped state access) before reaching for
orchestration machinery

00.0 Welcome to Multi-Agent Systems 📖
Learning objectives:
Recognize the class of problem that a single agent handles poorly and multiple agents handle well
Preview the three things this course delivers: the workflow mindset, the pattern landscape, and the
first concrete implementation step
Content outline:
The gap: you can build one agent that loops over tools. That agent works until the task grows — when
it needs deep expertise in several areas at once, or when its prompt swells with every possible
instruction until it starts making mistakes. That is the "todólogo" (do-it-all) agent, and it breaks under
its own weight.
Concrete contexts where multiple agents earn their place:
A customer-support system where a triage agent reads an incoming ticket and hands it to a
billing specialist, a technical-support specialist, or a returns specialist — each with its own
tools and instructions.
A content pipeline where a research agent gathers sources, a writer agent drafts from them,
and an editor agent tightens the draft — each output feeding the next.
A financial-report generator where an orchestrator splits a 10-K filing into sections, worker
agents summarize each section in parallel, and a synthesizer merges the summaries into one
brief.
A code-review assistant where one agent checks style, another scans for security issues,
and their findings are combined into a single review.
A travel-planning assistant that delegates flights, hotels, and the day-by-day itinerary to
focused sub-agents, then assembles the trip.
What this course covers (and what it deliberately does not): you'll build the mental model for multi-
agent design, learn to name the standard flow patterns (each gets its own dedicated course later),
and implement the concrete building block that every multi-agent graph rests on — the ToolNode
and tools that share graph state.
Key principles:


[Page 3]
Multi-agent design is a response to a specific pressure: one agent carrying too many responsibilities.
It is not automatically better — it is better when the problem demands it.
This course is the on-ramp: reason first, then take one concrete implementation step. The
orchestration machinery (routing graphs, parallel workers, evaluator loops, checkpointing) is built in
the courses that follow.
01.0 What Is an Agent Workflow 📖
Section goal: Build the mental model for multi-agent design — what an agent workflow is, the spectrum from
code-driven to LLM-driven control, and how to decide whether to split responsibilities and how to scope each
agent.
Learning objectives:
Define an agent workflow and place any system on the spectrum between "LLM embedded in
predefined code paths" and "LLM directs the control flow"
Decide when a single well-equipped agent suffices versus when to split responsibilities across agents
Apply the design rules that make split agents maintainable: one purpose each, explicit interfaces,
replaceability, and a stateless orchestrator
Content outline:
What an agent workflow is: a system where language models and tools are wired together through
a defined structure to accomplish a task. The key design question is how much control the LLM has over
the flow.
The control-flow spectrum (both ends are valid; the difference is who decides what happens next):
LLM embedded in predefined code paths — you, the developer, fix the sequence of steps in
code; the LLM fills in each step (classify this text, summarize that section). The path is
predetermined; the model supplies intelligence at each node. This is a workflow.
LLM directs control flow through predefined code paths — the model chooses which of
the available paths to take at each decision point (which tool to call, which agent to hand to).
The building blocks are still predefined, but the model steers the route through them. This is
agentic.
Most real systems sit between these poles: predictable structure with model-driven decisions
at specific junctions.
The core sizing decision — one agent or several? (howToThink)
A single agent with good tools is enough when the task is one coherent job and the tool set is
small and related. Reach for multiple agents when the work spans genuinely different kinds
of expertise, when one prompt would have to contain contradictory instructions, or when
parts of the job could run independently.
Determine the strategy per problem — there is no universal answer. The cost of an extra
agent (more model calls, more coordination) must be paid back by clearer responsibilities or
real parallelism.
Design rules for split agents (best practices, woven in):
One purpose per agent — planner, executor, verifier, orchestrator. Name the role; give it only
the tools and instructions that role needs. Never a generalist. (This is the Role Specialization
Pattern: each agent owns a bounded capability; you compose agents to cover the whole
workflow.)
Explicit, typed interfaces between agents — define what goes in and what comes out,
documented and typed. An agent's output should be a structured object another agent can


[Page 4]
consume without guessing. (The Structured Handoff Pattern: a handoff is a typed message
like {task, inputs, expected_output_schema} , not a natural-language instruction.)
Replaceable agents — swapping one agent's implementation should not force you to
rewrite the others. Interfaces make this possible.
Stateless orchestrator — the agent that routes and delegates should not itself execute
domain logic. It decides who does the work, not how the work is done.
Clear communication is what makes the flow succeed: agents that can't see the state they need, or
that exchange vague natural-language messages, drift and compound errors. The next section names
the standard shapes these workflows take.
Anti-patterns (woven in, each with its consequence):
The single "todólogo" agent — one agent with tools bolted on until it breaks. Complexity
without structure; the prompt becomes unmaintainable and the model's accuracy drops.
Blind agents — agents that act without knowing the state of the flow. They make decisions
on stale or missing context and produce work that doesn't fit.
An orchestrator that executes domain logic — it becomes a bottleneck and a single point
of failure, and it stops being replaceable.
Free-form natural language as the only protocol between agents — ambiguity
compounds at every hop; one misinterpretation cascades through the rest of the workflow.
Transitions: 01.0 establishes why and how to split work. 01.1 names the standard flow patterns that structure
these workflows.
Key principles:
Place any system on the control-flow spectrum first — it tells you how much you can rely on the
model versus the code.
Split responsibilities only when the problem demands it, and when you do, give each agent one
purpose, a typed interface, and independence from the others.
The orchestrator delegates; it does not do the work.
01.1 Flow Patterns 📖
Learning objectives:
Name the five standard flow patterns and state, in one line each, when to use them
Explain the difference between routing and orchestrator-worker — the distinction that most often
gets confused
Content outline:
Multi-agent workflows tend to take one of a handful of recognizable shapes. This lesson names them
so you can recognize which one a problem calls for; each pattern has its own dedicated course later
where you'll implement it. Here we only learn what each is and when to reach for it — no
implementation.
The five flow patterns (based on the LangChain workflows-and-agents guide):
Prompt chaining (sequential pipeline) — steps run strictly in order; each agent's output is
the next agent's input. Use it when the work is inherently sequential and each stage depends
on the one before (research → draft → edit). It is the simplest and most debuggable shape.
Parallelization — independent subtasks run at the same time and their results are
combined. Use it when the subtasks are truly independent (summarize five documents at
once). Do not parallelize for speed when outputs actually depend on each other — shared,
interdependent work corrupts under parallelism.


[Page 5]
Routing — one agent classifies the input and the workflow follows the branch that matches.
Use it when the path depends on the content of the LLM's output (a support ticket that is
"billing" versus "technical"). The LLM classifies; the graph sends the request down exactly one
path.
Orchestrator-worker — a central orchestrator decomposes a task into subtasks, delegates
each to a worker, and a synthesizer merges the results (the Orchestrator-Worker-
Synthesizer Pattern). Use it when the task must be broken into parts that are handled
separately and then reassembled (split a report into sections, summarize each, merge).
Evaluator-optimizer — a generator produces a result and an evaluator judges it, looping
until the result is accepted. Use it when quality can be checked and improved iteratively (draft,
critique, revise). The deep dive on this pattern is the very next skill in the arc; here it is named
only.
Routing vs. orchestration — the distinction to internalize (howToThink + anti-pattern):
Routing selects one path. The classifier picks a single destination and the request goes
there. Nothing is decomposed; one branch handles the whole request.
Orchestrator-worker decomposes into many. The orchestrator breaks the task into
multiple subtasks that are worked (often in parallel) and then merged. It is not choosing one
of several handlers — it is splitting one job across several.
They are not interchangeable. Using routing where orchestrator-worker is needed is a
classic mistake: you send a multi-part job down a single branch and one agent is stuck doing
work that should have been decomposed. Ask: "Does this pick one handler, or split the job
into parts?" — that answer tells you which pattern applies.
Choosing among them (best practices): prefer the simplest shape that fits — prompt chaining before
routing, routing before orchestration — because each added structure costs coordination and model
calls. Match the pattern to the shape of the problem, not to how sophisticated you want the system to
look.
Transitions: 01.1 names the patterns you'll orchestrate. Section 02 drops to the implementation floor: the
ToolNode , the building block every one of these graphs is made of.
Key principles:
Five shapes cover most multi-agent workflows: prompt chaining, parallelization, routing, orchestrator-
worker, evaluator-optimizer.
Routing picks one path; orchestrator-worker splits one job into many — confusing the two is the most
common structural error.
Reach for the simplest pattern that fits; added structure must earn its coordination cost.
02.0 From Tool Loops to ToolNode 📖
Section goal: Replace the hand-written tool-dispatch loop from the previous course with LangGraph's
ToolNode , and understand why shared graph state is the right coordination medium.
Learning objectives:
Explain what a ToolNode  does and why it replaces manual tool-dispatch logic
Wire a ToolNode  into a StateGraph  as the tool-execution step of an agent loop
Describe graph state as the shared blackboard that agents and tools coordinate through
Content outline:


[Page 6]
Recap of the manual loop (the starting point you already know): in the previous course you ran
the agent loop by hand — invoke the model, inspect the response for tool calls, dispatch each call
yourself, append the results, and invoke again:
from langchain.messages import HumanMessage, ToolMessage
available_tools = {"get_weather": get_weather, "search": search}
messages = [HumanMessage("What's the weather in Paris?")]
response = llm_with_tools.invoke(messages)
while response.tool_calls:
    messages.append(response)
    for call in response.tool_calls:
        result = available_tools[call["name"]].invoke(call["args"])
        messages.append(ToolMessage(result, tool_call_id=call["id"]))
    response = llm_with_tools.invoke(messages)
This works, but you own every fragile detail: looking up the tool by name, matching
tool_call_id s, appending in the right order, and handling a tool that raises.
ToolNode  as the evolution of tool-calling: LangGraph packages that entire dispatch step into one
prebuilt node. You hand it your list of tools; it reads the latest model message, runs every requested
tool call, captures errors, and writes the ToolMessage  results back into state:
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode
tool_node = ToolNode([get_weather, search])
The ToolNode  becomes the "tools" node in your graph. The model node decides whether to call
tools; the ToolNode  executes them and updates state consistently. (Best practice: prefer a
ToolNode  over a raw tool-calling loop — it handles dispatch, error capture, and state updates
uniformly, so you don't reimplement them per project.)
Graph state as the shared blackboard: in a LangGraph app, nodes don't pass values by calling each
other — they read from and write to a shared state object. The model node appends its response to
state; the ToolNode  reads that response from state and appends tool results back. This is the
Blackboard Pattern: agents and tools coordinate by reading and writing a shared state object rather
than talking directly. MessagesState  is the prebuilt state that carries the running messages  list;
you extend it when you need extra keys.
Structured handoffs over graph state: because the coordination medium is a typed state object,
handoffs between steps are structured data, not free-form text. A ToolNode  writing a
ToolMessage  back into messages  is a structured handoff — the next model invocation reads a
well-formed result, not a prose summary someone hoped it would parse correctly.
Transitions: 02.0 introduces the ToolNode  and the graph-state blackboard. 02.1 has you wire one into a
working agent graph.
Key principles:
A ToolNode  is the tool-execution step of an agent loop, packaged: it replaces the manual
dispatch/append/error-handling code you used to write by hand.
Nodes coordinate through shared graph state (the blackboard), not by calling each other directly.
Prefer the ToolNode  over a hand-rolled loop — consistent dispatch and error handling come for
free.


[Page 7]
02.1 Building a ToolNode Graph 💻
Challenge prompt: You are replacing a hand-written tool-dispatch loop with a proper LangGraph agent graph
that uses a ToolNode . Work in app.py , where a get_weather  tool, a ChatAnthropic  model bound to
that tool, and a call_model  node function are already provided.
Your task: assemble the graph so the model can call the tool and respond with the result.
Build a StateGraph  over MessagesState  with two nodes: "model"  (the provided
call_model  function) and "tools"  (a ToolNode  that runs get_weather ).
Wire the agent loop: an edge from START  into "model" , a conditional edge out of "model"
using the prebuilt tools_condition , and an edge from "tools"  back to "model" .
Compile the graph into a variable named graph .
Expected result: running app.py  invokes the graph with the question "Weather in Paris?"; the model calls
get_weather , the ToolNode  runs it, and the final printed message contains the weather sentence for
Paris (e.g. It is 22°C and sunny in Paris. ).
Solution code:
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, tools_condition
@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Return the current weather for a city."""
    return f"It is 22°C and sunny in {city}."
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6")
llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools([get_weather])
def call_model(state: MessagesState) -> dict:
    return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke(state["messages"])]}
builder = StateGraph(MessagesState)
builder.add_node("model", call_model)
builder.add_node("tools", ToolNode([get_weather]))
builder.add_edge(START, "model")
builder.add_conditional_edges("model", tools_condition)
builder.add_edge("tools", "model")
graph = builder.compile()
result = graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in 
Paris?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
Challenge code:


[Page 8]
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, tools_condition
@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Return the current weather for a city."""
    return f"It is 22°C and sunny in {city}."
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6")
llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools([get_weather])
def call_model(state: MessagesState) -> dict:
    return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke(state["messages"])]}
# Build a StateGraph over MessagesState with two nodes:
#   "model" -> call_model, and "tools" -> a ToolNode that runs get_weather.
# Wire START -> "model", a conditional edge from "model" using tools_condition,
# and an edge from "tools" back to "model". Compile into `graph`.

Paris?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
Observable output: the script prints the model's final message, which reports the weather for Paris — proof
the ToolNode  executed get_weather  and the result flowed back to the model. If the graph is wired wrong
(missing conditional edge or the tools → model  edge), the run errors or the tool result never reaches the
model.
03.0 Tools and Graph State 📖
Section goal: Let tools read from and write to graph state directly through the ToolRuntime  parameter, and
scope each tool to only the state it needs.
Learning objectives:
Give a tool access to graph state and run context via the ToolRuntime  parameter
Write a tool that updates graph state by returning a Command
Scope each tool to the minimal state slice it needs, and version the state schema at the boundary
Content outline:
The problem: some tools need information that isn't in the model's arguments — the current user's
id, an account tier, a running total — values that live in graph state. Passing them as tool arguments
would force the model to know and repeat them; instead the tool should read them straight from
state.
Reading state with ToolRuntime : declare a runtime: ToolRuntime  parameter on the tool.
LangGraph injects it automatically — it never appears in the schema the model sees, so the model
doesn't (and can't) fill it in:


[Page 9]
from langchain.tools import tool, ToolRuntime
@tool
def get_user_orders(runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str:
    """List the current user's recent orders."""
    user_id = runtime.state["user_id"]        # read from graph state
    return f"Recent orders for {user_id}: #1021, #1044."
The runtime also exposes run-scoped context ( runtime.context.some_field ), the persistent
store ( runtime.store ), and the current runtime.tool_call_id  — the id you pair a result back
to.
Writing to state with Command : a tool updates graph state by returning a
Command(update=...) . This writes the given keys back into state and, because the tool is running
inside the graph, must also emit its ToolMessage  so the conversation stays well-formed:
from langgraph.types import Command
from langchain.messages import ToolMessage
@tool
def set_shipping_preference(value: str, runtime: ToolRuntime) -> Command:
    """Save the customer's shipping preference into graph state."""
    return Command(update={
        "shipping_preference": value,
        "messages": [ToolMessage("Preference saved.", 
tool_call_id=runtime.tool_call_id)],
    })
A tool that reads and writes state directly is exactly what the "ToolNode como evolución del
ToolCalling" step buys you: tools become first-class participants in the shared blackboard.
Scope each tool to the state it needs (Scoped Context Pattern + best practices): a tool should read
only the state keys it declares as dependencies — get_user_orders  reads user_id , not the
entire conversation history. Before invoking an agent, project the full state down to the minimal
context that agent requires. Design per-agent context windows explicitly.
Type the boundary and version the schema (best practices): the extra state keys a tool relies on are
a typed contract — define them on your state TypedDict / MessagesState  subclass. When agents
evolve independently, a change to one agent's output can silently break a downstream reader;
version the state/message schema so a mismatch is caught at the boundary instead of corrupting a
run.
Anti-patterns (woven in, each with its consequence):
Accessing the full conversation history from every tool — tools should read only the keys
they depend on; pulling the whole history bloats context, slows the tool, and couples it to
unrelated state.
Passing full conversation history to every agent — context bloat degrades reasoning
quality and raises latency; give each agent the slice it needs.
Agents/tools without defined output schemas — downstream readers get ambiguous
input and hallucinate an interpretation.
No schema versioning — one agent's output format changes and every downstream reader
breaks silently.
Shared mutable state with no access control — multiple writers hitting the same key
without coordination corrupt the state; the orchestrator should govern who may write what.


[Page 10]
(This is also why you never parallelize agents that share mutable state — race conditions
corrupt the graph state.)
Transitions: 03.0 shows how tools read and write shared state. 03.1 has you write a tool that reads a state
value through ToolRuntime .
Key principles:
Tools reach graph state and run context through an injected runtime: ToolRuntime  — hidden
from the model, available to your code.
Read only the state keys a tool depends on (scoped context); write state back with
Command(update=...) .
Type the state boundary and version the schema so independent agents don't break each other
silently.
03.1 Reading State From a Tool 💻
Challenge prompt: An order-status assistant needs a tool that estimates shipping time based on the
customer's account tier — a value that lives in the graph's state, not in the model's request. Work in app.py ,
where a State  (a MessagesState  subclass with an account_tier  key), a ChatAnthropic  model, a
call_model  node, and the full graph wiring are already provided.
Your task: implement the missing get_shipping_estimate  tool so it reads the tier from graph state
through the runtime.
Define get_shipping_estimate  as a @tool  whose only parameter is runtime: ToolRuntime
(no other arguments — the model must not supply the tier).
Read account_tier  from the graph state via runtime.state .
Return "Estimated shipping: 1 business day(s) for a premium customer."  when the tier
is "premium" , and the same sentence with 5  day(s) and the actual tier otherwise.
Expected result: running app.py  invokes the graph with account_tier  set to "premium" ; the model
calls the tool, which reads the tier from state and returns the 1-day estimate, so the final printed message
reflects premium shipping. Changing account_tier  to "standard"  yields the 5-day estimate — the
model never passes the tier, proving the tool read it from state.
Solution code:
from langchain.tools import tool, ToolRuntime
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, tools_condition
class State(MessagesState):
    account_tier: str
@tool
def get_shipping_estimate(runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str:
    """Estimate shipping time for the current customer."""
    tier = runtime.state["account_tier"]
    days = 1 if tier == "premium" else 5
    return f"Estimated shipping: {days} business day(s) for a {tier} customer."


[Page 11]
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6")
llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools([get_shipping_estimate])
def call_model(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke(state["messages"])]}

04.0 Multi-Agent Systems Assessment 🧠
Learning objectives evaluated:
The agent-workflow control-flow spectrum
When to split responsibilities and how to scope agents
The five flow patterns and the routing-vs-orchestration distinction
ToolNode  as the evolution of manual tool dispatch
Tools reading graph state via ToolRuntime  and scoped context
Questions:
Question 1 A workflow is described as "the LLM directs control flow through predefined code paths." What
does that mean?
A) The developer hard-codes the exact sequence of steps and the model only fills in each step's content. B) The
building blocks are predefined, but at each decision point the model chooses which path to take. C) The model
writes new code paths at runtime that did not exist before. D) There is no structure at all — the model does
whatever it wants with no predefined nodes.
Correct: B — the paths (nodes, tools, agents) are predefined; what makes it agentic is that the model decides
which of them to use at each junction. Option A describes the other end of the spectrum (LLM embedded in
fixed paths). Options C and D overstate the model's freedom.
Question 2 You're building a system to answer support tickets. A single agent's prompt has grown to include
billing rules, technical troubleshooting steps, and return-policy logic, and it's starting to mix them up. What
does this signal?
A) The model is too small — switch to a larger model and keep one agent. B) You've hit the "todólogo" anti-
pattern; split responsibilities into agents with one purpose each. C) You should remove the tools so the
prompt is shorter. D) Nothing — one agent with a long prompt is the recommended design.
Correct: B — a single do-it-all agent accumulating contradictory instructions until accuracy drops is the classic
anti-pattern. The fix is role specialization: one purpose per agent (a billing agent, a technical agent, a returns
agent), each scoped to its own tools and instructions.
Question 3 What is the key difference between routing and the orchestrator-worker pattern?
A) Routing decomposes a task into parallel subtasks; orchestrator-worker picks one handler. B) They are
interchangeable names for the same pattern. C) Routing selects one path for the request; orchestrator-worker
splits one job into multiple subtasks and merges the results. D) Routing requires a checkpointer; orchestrator-
worker does not.


[Page 13]
Correct: C — routing classifies and sends the request down a single branch; orchestrator-worker decomposes
one job into several subtasks (often run in parallel) and synthesizes them. Option A reverses the two; using
routing where decomposition is needed is a common structural mistake.
Question 4 Why does a ToolNode  replace the hand-written tool-dispatch loop from a basic agent?
A) It makes the model call tools faster by skipping the model entirely. B) It packages tool lookup, execution,
error capture, and writing results back into state into one prebuilt node. C) It removes the need for a model in
the graph. D) It stores tool results in a database automatically.
Correct: B — a ToolNode  takes your list of tools and handles the dispatch step consistently: read the latest
model message, run each tool call, capture errors, and append the ToolMessage  results to state. It doesn't
replace the model or add persistence.
Question 5 A tool needs the current user's account_tier , which lives in graph state — not in the model's
request. What is the correct LangGraph 1.x way to read it?
A) Add account_tier  as a normal tool argument so the model passes it in. B) Declare a runtime:
ToolRuntime  parameter and read runtime.state["account_tier"] . C) Import the global graph object
and read its .state  attribute directly. D) Parse the value out of the conversation history inside the tool.
Correct: B — a runtime: ToolRuntime  parameter is injected automatically and hidden from the model;
runtime.state  exposes the graph state. Making it a model argument (A) forces the model to know and
repeat the value; C and D are fragile and unsupported.
Question 6 Why should a tool read only the specific state keys it depends on, instead of the full conversation
history?
A) Reading full history is impossible in LangGraph. B) It keeps each tool scoped and cheap: less context bloat,
lower latency, and no coupling to unrelated state. C) The full history is encrypted and cannot be read by tools.
D) Tools are not allowed to read state at all.
Correct: B — the Scoped Context Pattern: give each tool only the slice it needs. Pulling the entire history
bloats context, degrades reasoning quality, raises latency, and couples the tool to state it shouldn't care about.
Reading state (scoped) is fully supported, so C and D are wrong.
